meta.descriptionEn: On 24 September 2014, a small Indian probe fired its engine after ten months in deep space and a nation held its breath. Mangalyaan, built in just 15 months for about ₹450 crore, had one chance to enter Mars orbit. Only one space agency had ever succeeded on a first attempt. How did ISRO pull it off with a weaker rocket, a faulty burn and a tiny budget? And what did the little orbiter discover in its eight years around the Red Planet, from Martian argon to the Sun's corona? This documentary follows the mission from a rocket switch and delayed launch, through a nerve-racking engine problem, to its silent final chapter in 2022.
meta.descriptionUr: 24 September 2014 ko ek chhota Indian probe das mahine ke khamosh safar ke baad Mars ke qareeb apna engine chalane wala tha, aur poori qaum saans roke dekh rahi thi. Mangalyaan sirf 15 mahine mein, taqreeban 450 crore rupay mein bana tha. ISRO ne kamzor rocket aur engine ke masle ke bawajood yeh kaise kiya? Mars ke aath saalon mein is probe ne kya kya dhoonda? Is documentary mein poori kahani Urdu aur English mein dekhiye.

articleEn: It is 24 September 2014. At the ISTRAC Spacecraft Control Centre in Bengaluru, India, engineers are watching a spacecraft that is about to enter Mars orbit. It has travelled for 298 days to get here. Now its 440 newton engine must slow it down so that it can be captured by Mars. Two days earlier, on 22 September, that engine was test-fired for just 3.968 seconds, less than four seconds.

If all goes well, ISRO will become the fourth space agency in the world to reach Mars orbit, and India will be the first Asian country to do so. But this mission is not only a story of success. How was all this achieved on such a small budget? Why was a less powerful rocket chosen? Why was the launch delayed? What problem did the engine show along the way? And what did the orbiter discover at Mars?

The biggest question comes last: why did the orbiter fall silent eight years later? The answer comes at the end. In this video we will look at how the idea of Mangalyaan was born, how it was built, and what it saw at Mars. So let us go to that day, when everything depended on one short burn. Friends, the story begins.

articleEn: The story of Mangalyaan begins not at Mars but at the Moon. In 2008 ISRO launched a lunar satellite named Chandrayaan-1. In November of that same year, the then ISRO chairman G. Madhavan Nair publicly announced an uncrewed mission to Mars for the first time. In 2010 the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology carried out a feasibility study of the idea, and the dream began to take shape. On 3 August 2012, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh approved the project. Before that, ISRO had already completed ₹125 crore worth of necessary studies.

According to reports, the total cost of the project could reach ₹454 crore. The satellite itself cost ₹153 crore, and the rest was to be spent on ground stations and relay upgrades. But ISRO was no new organisation. Its roots go back to INCOSPAR, formed in 1962 on the suggestion of Vikram Sarabhai. In 1975 Aryabhata, the first satellite built by ISRO, was launched on a Soviet rocket. In 1980 the satellite RS-1 went into orbit on India's own SLV-3 rocket. The PSLV arrived in the 1990s. Apart from its first flight and two partial failures, it built a record of more than 50 successful flights.

After Chandrayaan-1, a new question arose: could India reach another planet with its own technology? The main aim of the Mars Orbiter Mission was technology more than science. It was a technology demonstrator, meant to learn how to design, plan and operate an interplanetary mission. That included leaving Earth orbit, following a heliocentric path, and finally being captured into Mars orbit. The team also had to build orbit and attitude models, navigate throughout the mission, and include autonomous features for difficult situations.

The second aim was scientific: to study the Martian surface, its morphology and mineralogy, and to examine components of its atmosphere such as methane and CO2. The mission was also meant to help understand Mars's upper atmosphere, the effects of the solar wind, and the escape of gases into space.

There was also a timing issue. The chance to use a fuel-saving Hohmann transfer orbit to Mars comes every 26 months, so missing it means a long wait. Approval was granted and the goals were set. But the hardest question remained: how quickly could this probe be built?

articleEn: The answer was 15 months. At the ISRO Satellite Centre, development of the spacecraft was fast-tracked and completed in a record 15 months. The work was led by the Centre's Director, S. K. Shivakumar, who handled the concept, design and realization of the spacecraft. One reason for the speed was a reconfigured Chandrayaan-2 orbiter bus. Its structure was like that of Chandrayaan-1, with improvements for Mars.

At launch the spacecraft's total mass was 1,337.2 kg, including 852 kg of propellant. Its dry mass was only 482.5 kg. A 440 newton liquid engine handled orbit changes and Mars insertion, and eight 22 newton thrusters kept its orientation under control. Three solar panels supplied power, each measuring 1.8 metres by 1.4 metres, producing a maximum of 840 watts in Mars orbit. This power was stored in a 36 Ah lithium-ion battery, which will become very important later in this story.

For communications there were low gain, mid gain and high gain antennas. The high gain antenna used a 2.2 metre reflector and worked in S-band. The scientific payload was just 15 kg and included five instruments, whose mounting was completed at the U. R. Rao Satellite Centre in Bengaluru.

Many people stood behind the mission. K. Radhakrishnan was ISRO's chairman, Mylswamy Annadurai was programme director, and Subbiah Arunan was project director. Women scientists were part of the team too. Moumita Dutta was a project manager, while Nandini Harinath and Ritu Karidhal were deputy operations directors.

Then comes the question of cost. According to sources, the mission cost about ₹450 crore, and it was described as the cheapest Mars mission to date. In dollars, the figure varies between sources: 73 million in some, 74 million in others, and 47 million in one. So we will stick to the rupee figures.

According to ISRO chairman K. Radhakrishnan, the reasons for the low cost included a modular approach, fewer ground tests, and scientists working long days of 18 to 20 hours. BBC's Jonathan Amos pointed to low labour costs, the country's own technology, a simple design, and a payload less complex than that of NASA's MAVEN. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the mission cost only ₹7 per kilometre, cheaper than an auto ride in Ahmedabad at ₹10 per kilometre.
So the probe was ready. But the story of the rocket that would carry it to Mars is even more interesting. Why did the first choice have to change?

articleEn: PSLV was not ISRO's first choice. It wanted to send this mission on its Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, the GSLV. But in 2010 the GSLV failed twice, and its cryogenic engine still had problems. Waiting for newer rockets would have meant a delay of at least three years. So ISRO decided to go with the less powerful PSLV.

The problem was that the PSLV was not powerful enough to put MOM directly on course for Mars. A new approach was needed. The spacecraft would first be placed in a very long elliptical Earth orbit. Then it would fire its thrusters in several perigee burns to take advantage of the Oberth effect.

The rocket was called PSLV-XL C25. Its assembly began on 5 August 2013, and the complete spacecraft was sent to Sriharikota on 2 October 2013. Around that time there was another worry: a federal government shutdown was under way in the United States. Would NASA still help? On 5 October 2013, NASA reconfirmed that it would support communications and navigation through its Deep Space Network.

The launch date was first set for 28 October 2013, but ISRO's tracking ships were delayed by bad weather in the Pacific. On 19 October, ISRO chairman K. Radhakrishnan announced that the launch would move a week later. An important telemetry ship had been delayed in reaching Fiji. The new date became 5 November 2013.

At the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, the PSLV-XL stood ready on the first launch pad. At 09:08 UTC the rocket lifted off. By 09:50 UTC the satellite was in Earth orbit, and its antenna and all three solar panels had deployed. The orbit had a perigee of 264.1 kilometres, an apogee of 23,903.6 kilometres, and an inclination of 19.20 degrees. The destination was still very far away.

Remember that a fuel-saving Hohmann transfer window to Mars comes every 26 months, and the next two chances were in 2016 and 2018. The orbiter's dry mass was 482.5 kilos, and at launch it carried 852 kilos of fuel. This fuel was what it would use to escape Earth's grip. Could the small rocket really manage it? To find out, we have to look at the orbit raising burns of the coming days.

articleEn: The launch took place on 5 November, but the journey had only just begun. Now several burns had to be carried out around Earth, each making the orbit larger. All these operations were run from the Spacecraft Control Centre of the ISRO Telemetry Tracking and Command Network in Peenya, Bengaluru. They used the spacecraft's own 440 newton liquid engine, which burns monomethylhydrazine and dinitrogen tetroxide.

The first burn took place on 6 November at 19:47 UTC. The engine ran for 416 seconds, and the apogee rose to 28,825 kilometres, while the perigee stayed at 252 kilometres. The second burn followed the next day at 20:48 UTC. A 570.6 second burn raised the apogee to 40,186 kilometres. The third burn came on 8 November at 20:40 UTC. It lasted 707 seconds and took the apogee to 71,636 kilometres. The first three burns also tested the systems.

Then came the fourth burn, on 10 November. Its delta-v was only 35 m/s, while the plan called for 135 m/s. The motor had pushed less than expected. As a result the apogee reached only 78,276 kilometres instead of 100,000. Had the mission got stuck there? The cause was a test: the team was checking the built-in redundancies of the propulsion system. During this, the engine's flow stopped. When both the primary and redundant coils of the solenoid flow control valve were energised together, the flow shut off. In future the two coils could not be used together, but they could be fired separately, one after the other.

On 12 November ISRO carried out an additional unscheduled burn. The apogee rose to 118,642 kilometres, slightly more than the original target of the fourth burn. The final orbit raising manoeuvre took place on 15 November at 19:57 UTC, and the apogee reached 192,874 kilometres. One source also gives the date as 16 November. In all, six burns were completed in Earth orbit. A seventh burn, planned for 30 November, would send MOM away from Earth.

Tracking was also a challenge throughout this period. ISTRAC's ground stations were in Sriharikota, Port Blair, Brunei and Biak in Indonesia. Once the apogee went beyond 100,000 kilometres, the 18 metre and 32 metre antennas of the Indian Deep Space Network were used. The 18 metre dish was used for communication until April 2014, after which the larger 32 metre dish took over. When ISRO's network could not see the spacecraft, NASA's Deep Space Network stations at Canberra, Madrid and Goldstone supplied position data. South Africa's SANSA Hartebeesthoek ground station also provided tracking, telemetry and command services.
Now Earth's grip was about to break. But would this final push put MOM on its way to Mars?

articleEn: On 30 November 2013 at 19:19 UTC, another decisive moment arrived. The engine ran for 23 minutes. This firing took MOM out of its orbit around Earth and put it on a heliocentric orbit toward Mars, a path around the Sun. Six burns had already been done in Earth orbit, and this seventh burn set MOM free. The journey had now begun.

Consider that the whole route was 780,000,000 kilometres long. The total transit time was 298 days, about ten months. On such a long trip it is not easy to keep going straight, so four trajectory correction manoeuvres, or TCMs, were planned in advance.

The first TCM took place on 11 December 2013 at 01:00 UTC. The 22 newton thrusters were fired for 40.5 seconds. After that, MOM followed its designed path so closely that the correction planned for April 2014 was not needed at all. The second TCM took place on 11 June 2014 at 11:00 UTC, when the same 22 newton thrusters were fired for just 16 seconds. The third planned correction was also postponed, because the orbiter's trajectory was very close to plan. So only three of the four were carried out. The third correction actually took the form of the 3.9 second deceleration test on 22 September 2014, just two days before Mars.

For communications the spacecraft had a high-gain antenna, based on a 2.2 metre reflector, which sends and receives data in S-band. It also had low-gain and medium-gain antennas, and two 230-watt TWTAs and two coherent transponders handled communications.

The plan was for Mars orbit insertion on 24 September 2014. That was about two days after NASA's MAVEN orbiter was due to arrive. Spacecraft from two different countries were approaching Mars at almost the same time, with only two days between them. Now there was only waiting. After the long, silent flight, the 440 newton engine was to be tested on 22 September. Would it work?

articleEn: The moment that had been awaited for 298 days had arrived. On 22 September at 09:00 UTC, the 440 newton liquid apogee motor was fired for a test. The engine ran for only 3.968 seconds, less than four seconds. The test took place about 41 hours before the actual orbit insertion. The question was simple: had the engine woken up?

After the test, on 24 September 2014, the spacecraft performed a reverse manoeuvre. After the deceleration burn it corrected its orientation again, and with that, Mangalyaan entered Martian orbit. The date of 24 September 2014 was written into ISRO's history for good.

The insertion put MOM into a very long elliptical orbit around Mars, exactly as planned. Its period was 72 hours 51 minutes 51 seconds. The periapsis, the closest point to Mars, was 421.7 km away, and the apoapsis, the farthest point, was 76,993.6 km. The spacecraft came close at times and moved far away at others. After the insertion was complete, 40 kg of fuel remained on the spacecraft. Only 20 kg was needed for a six-month mission, so that was twice what was required.

With this, ISRO became the fourth space agency in the world to reach Mars orbit. Before it, the Soviet space program, NASA and ESA had done so. India became the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit, and it did so on its first attempt. That was no easy feat. Before this, only the European Space Agency had succeeded on a first attempt, in 2003, using a Roscosmos Soyuz/Fregat rocket. So ISRO became the second national agency to do so.

On 28 September 2014, the MOM team released the first global image of Mars, taken by the Mars Colour Camera. It was the mission's first big visual glimpse. In 2014 China described India's successful Mars mission as the Pride of Asia. In 2015 America's National Space Society gave the MOM team the Space Pioneer Award, because the Mars mission had succeeded on the very first try.
Friends, the images and honours were only the beginning. The question was what this small orbiter was actually going to tell us about Mars.

articleEn: The first test came as soon as MOM reached Mars. On 19 October 2014 the comet Siding Spring passed close to Mars, so ISRO kept the spacecraft behind Mars. The orbit was changed on 7 October, using 1.9 kg of fuel, and the apoapsis dropped to 72,000 km. After the comet passed, ISRO said MOM was fine.

Then it was science's turn. The instrument MENCA, the Mars Exospheric Neutral Composition Analyser, was measuring Mars's exosphere. In four orbits in December 2014, when the periapsis was lowest, MENCA built profiles of argon-40. Their scale height came out at about 16 km, which gives an exospheric temperature of about 275 K. But in two orbits the scale height increased noticeably, and the effective temperature rose above 400 K. NASA's MAVEN, with its NGIMS instrument, also saw a change in the slope of argon around 230 to 260 km. So the results of the two missions were similar.
Between 18 and 29 December 2014, MENCA measured the exosphere in the evening hours. Above 270 km, atomic oxygen becomes more abundant than carbon dioxide.

The Methane Sensor for Mars, or MSM, mapped Mars's reflectivity, or albedo. In the Tharsis plateau, Arabia Terra and Elysium Planitia, the albedo was above 0.4. These are regions generally covered by dust. In darker regions such as Syrtis Major Planum and Valles Marineris, the albedo was below 0.15.

Using stereo images from the Mars Colour Camera, atmospheric optical depth was measured on the northern wall of Valles Marineris. In the red channel it was 1.7 at the bottom and about 1.0 at the top. On the southern wall, however, the optical depth stayed between about 1.75 and 1.85 and did not decrease with height. This difference was important. There is a mountain-like structure there, on whose lee side lee wave clouds can form. The results support the presence of such clouds near 65°W.

In May and June 2015, Mars and Earth were on opposite sides of the Sun. MOM's 2.29 GHz S-band signals passed through the Sun's corona to reach Earth, giving scientists a chance to measure the Sun's atmosphere. At distances under 10 solar radii the turbulence spectrum flattened, a sign of the solar wind's acceleration region.

MOM also looked at Mars's moons. On 1 July 2020 it took a picture of Phobos from a distance of 4,200 km. The same spacecraft also gave the first views of the far side of Deimos. Such images had never been seen before.

On 24 September 2015, ISRO released a 120-page Mars Atlas containing images and data from the first year. The November 2016 cover of National Geographic magazine also carried a MOM image, with a story titled Mars: Race to the Red Planet.

On 17 January 2017, the eight 22 N thrusters fired for 431 seconds. 20 kg of propellant was used and 13 kg remained, and eclipses were avoided until September 2017. In this way the mission went far beyond its six-month design. On 24 September 2018 it completed four years, and by 2019 it had sent 2 terabytes of imaging data to Earth.

articleEn: After so many years of work, MOM was about to face something it had never been built for: a very long eclipse. During an eclipse the spacecraft moves into Mars's shadow, and the solar panels get no sunlight. The system then runs on its battery, which was 36 Ah. In January 2017 ISRO had changed the orbit to try to avoid eclipses. The reason was clear: the battery could handle eclipses of at most 100 minutes.

Then April 2022 came. By then the spacecraft faced gradually longer eclipses, including one lasting 7 hours. Then communication was lost. According to ISRO, contact ended in April 2022, but the world learned of it on 2 October 2022. According to the report, the orbiter had lost contact with Earth for good.
The next day ISRO's statement came: all attempts at recovery had failed. ISRO formally declared MOM dead. A mission designed for six months had circled Mars for more than seven years.

When contact was lost, the cause was not known. One possibility was that power ran out, another was that during automatic manoeuvres the Earth-facing antenna turned away by mistake. Later ISRO's estimate emerged that the spacecraft's attitude control propellant had probably run out, so it could not be recovered. At the eighth anniversary conference on 27 September, the point under discussion was that without fuel, attitude adjustment was no longer possible, and that adjustment was needed to keep battery power up.
Possibly the shortage of fuel and the long eclipse together ended the mission. So was this a failure? Or the natural end of a mission that did many times more work than its design life?

articleEn: So was it a failure or a success? Perhaps the answer lies in the mission's legacy. Let us see what Mangalyaan left behind. In 2015 the National Space Society gave the MOM team the Space Pioneer Award, because the Mars mission succeeded on its first attempt. The back of India's ₹2,000 note carries a picture of the Mars Orbiter Mission spacecraft. The cover of National Geographic's November 2016 issue was also a MOM image. And the 2019 Hindi film Mission Mangal was loosely inspired by this mission.

On 30 September 2014, officials of NASA and ISRO signed an agreement aimed at paving the way to explore Mars together in the future. One aim of this working group was also to look at the possibility of coordinated observations and science analysis between the MAVEN orbiter and MOM.

What next? ISRO wants to work on a follow-up Mars Lander Mission, or Mangalyaan-2. But sources do not agree on its launch date. One source says it will go in 2027, with the orbiter using aerobraking to reduce its apoapsis. Another source calls it proposed for 2030. The 2030 plan mentions a rover, a helicopter, a sky crane and a supersonic parachute. This time the intention is not just to orbit, but to reach the surface. On 23 August 2023, Chandrayaan-3 made a soft landing near the Moon's south pole, and ISRO became the first space agency to do so.

The first lesson is frugal engineering. According to Radhakrishnan, the modular approach, fewer ground tests and 18 to 20 hour workdays kept costs down. The second lesson is about design margins. The battery could handle eclipses of only 100 minutes, while in April 2022 a seven-hour eclipse arrived. And the mission's design life was only six months, yet MOM worked for about eight years. The cost was about ₹450 crore.

Many questions are still open. When communication was lost, it was not known whether power ran out or an automatic manoeuvre turned the antenna away. So is a big success possible at a low cost? shorts.text: صرف 3.968 seconds! کیا اتنا مختصر test ایک پورے Mars mission کی قسمت بتا سکتا ہے؟ 22 September 2014 کو ISRO نے spacecraft کا 440 newton والا engine اتنی ہی دیر چلایا۔ یہ test اصل orbit insertion سے تقریباً 41 گھنٹے پہلے ہوا۔ Spacecraft 298 دن کا سفر کر چکا تھا۔ پھر 24 September آیا۔ Bengaluru کے Spacecraft Control Centre میں سب کی نظریں screens پر تھیں۔ Engine کو spacecraft کی رفتار کم کرنی تھی، تاکہ وہ Mars کے orbit میں داخل ہو سکے۔ اگر سب ٹھیک رہتا، تو ISRO دنیا کی چوتھی space agency بن جاتی جو Mars کے orbit تک پہنچی۔ اور India پہلا Asian ملک ہوتا۔ لیکن ایک سوال باقی تھا۔ کیا engine واقعی کام کرے گا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sirf 3.968 seconds! Kya itna mukhtasar test aik poore Mars mission ki qismat bata sakta hai? 22 September 2014 ko ISRO ne spacecraft ka 440 newton wala engine itni hi der chalaya. Yeh test asal orbit insertion se taqriban 41 ghantay pehle hua. Spacecraft 298 din ka safar kar chuka tha. Phir 24 September aaya. Bengaluru ke Spacecraft Control Centre mein sab ki nazrein screens par thin. Engine ko spacecraft ki raftaar kam karni thi, taake woh Mars ke orbit mein dakhil ho sake. Agar sab theek rehta, to ISRO duniya ki chauthi space agency ban jati jo Mars ke orbit tak pohanchi. Aur India pehla Asian mulk hota. Lekin aik sawal baqi tha. Kya engine waqai kaam karega? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

Could that tiny test decide the fate of India's first Mars mission?

shorts.titleEn: The Burn That Fell Short: Mangalyaan's Fourth Manoeuvre
shorts.text: منصوبہ تھا 135 m/s کا۔ ملا صرف 35 m/s! 10 November 2013 کو MOM کا چوتھا orbit raising burn شروع ہوا۔ Spacecraft Earth کے گرد اپنا orbit بڑا کر رہا تھا۔ Apogee کو 100,000 km تک جانا تھا۔ مگر engine کم چلا، اور apogee صرف 78,276 km تک پہنچا۔ وجہ کیا تھی؟ ISRO کے مطابق redundancy test کے دوران valve کے primary اور redundant دونوں coils ایک ساتھ energise ہوئے، اور engine کا flow رک گیا۔ تو کیا mission یہیں ختم ہو گیا؟ نہیں۔ 12 November کو ایک اضافی burn کیا گیا، اور apogee 118,642 km ہو گیا۔ یہ اصل منصوبے سے بھی کچھ اونچا تھا۔ مگر اصل امتحان تو ابھی باقی تھا۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Mansooba tha 135 m/s ka. Mila sirf 35 m/s! 10 November 2013 ko MOM ka chautha orbit raising burn shuru hua. Spacecraft Earth ke gird apna orbit bara kar raha tha. Apogee ko 100,000 km tak jana tha. Magar engine kam chala, aur apogee sirf 78,276 km tak pohancha. Wajah kya thi? ISRO ke mutabiq redundancy test ke dauran valve ke primary aur redundant dono coils aik sath energise hue, aur engine ka flow ruk gaya. To kya mission yahin khatam ho gaya? Nahin. 12 November ko aik izafi burn kiya gaya, aur apogee 118,642 km ho gaya. Yeh asal mansoobe se bhi kuch ooncha tha. Magar asal imtihan to abhi baqi tha. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 10 November 2013, Mangalyaan's fourth orbit-raising burn delivered 35 m/s instead of the planned 135 m/s.
An extra burn two days later raised the apogee to 118,642 km and kept the mission on track.

Isi liye January 2017 mein ISRO ne orbit badla tha. Phir April 2022 aaya. Eclipses aahista aahista lambay hotay gaye, jin mein saat ghantay ka aik eclipse bhi tha. Is ke baad Earth se rabta toot gaya. Rabta April 2022 mein khatam hua, magar khabar 2 October 2022 ko samnay aayi. Akhir wahan kya hua tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

In April 2022, Mangalyaan faced a seven-hour eclipse its 36 Ah battery was never designed to survive.
Communication was lost, and ISRO later declared the orbiter unrecoverable.
